item.title: Two faced remarks by Philippine diplomat expose Manila's bid to exploit Taiwan question for S.China Sea interests; Political ploy will not succeed
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 13:33:00
Illustration: Liu Rui/GT A Philippine diplomat's recent remarks that the Philippines is exploring deeper cooperation with the Taiwan region on protecting undersea cables, "notwithstanding the one-China policy," expose the Marcos Jr. government's ulterior motive of playing the Taiwan card to gain leverage in the South China Sea. Such duplicitous words and actions amount to a deceptive political ploy that will not succeed, said a Chinese expert, noting that the Philippines will ultimately reap what it sows and its moves to heighten cross-Strait tensions and persist in provocations in the South China Sea will only backfire. The Philippines is exploring deeper cooperation with Taiwan on protecting undersea cables and addressing "gray-zone" activity, "despite Manila's one-China policy." Felipe F. Carino III, Manila's deputy chief of mission in Washington, told a seminar on Wednesday this "pragmatic and practical approach" with Taiwan was necessary to protect mutual interests in the Bashi Channel between Taiwan region and the Philippines, according to a Reuters report. Speaking to Washington's Center for a New American Security, Carino linked cable security to South China Sea tensions, but did not mention China by name. "We are exploring deeper cooperation with our friends in Taiwan," Carino claimed, adding that the Philippines was doing so "notwithstanding our one China policy," according to the report. Asked if this cooperation could include joint patrols or accountability for vessels that disrupt communications, Carino said he did not have details, but said: "I'm sure that this is a constantly evolving cooperation, and some of the things that you mentioned may be actually coming to fruition," per Reuters. The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities in the Taiwan region initially hyped the undersea cable issue, making false accusations against the Chinese mainland. Philippine diplomats are now exploiting it to stoke the "China threat" narrative, bolster their defenses and play the "Taiwan card" to secure US support, ultimately seeking leverage in the South China Sea, Zheng Jian, a professor at the Taiwan Research Institute of Xiamen University, told the Global Times on Thursday. The Marcos Jr. administration is playing the Taiwan card to draw in the US, link South China Sea issues with the Taiwan question, and integrate the Philippines into the US first-island-chain defense strategy to contain China, said Zheng, noting that by paying lip services to the one-China principle while pursuing highly sensitive security cooperation with the Taiwan region, Manila seeks to conceal its intentions and evade international scrutiny. "But such a deceptive political ploy will not succeed," said the expert. According to a report from the Nikkei Asia on Monday, Taiwan region and the Philippines "are taking steps to boost maritime ties after decades of distance" amid rising pressure from Chinese vessels. A Taipei Times report on Wednesday noted that the Taiwan region coast guard administration donated a patrol vessel - 500-tonne-class Kinmen to the Philippines, but it will not be used in waters near Taiwan region. Recent interactions between the Philippines and the DPP authorities in the Taiwan region reflect political calculations on both sides. However, pursuing so-called security or even military cooperation in defiance of the one-China principle crosses red lines and will inevitably draw firm opposition and countermeasures from the Chinese mainland, experts warned. Zheng said Manila's attempts to link South China Sea issues with the Taiwan question risk drawing the Philippines into a cross-Strait conflict through its cooperation with the Taiwan region. By tying its national interests to external forces, the Philippines will ultimately bear the consequences, he said. The Chinese mainland market remains vital to Philippine development. Yet some Philippine politicians prioritize geopolitical confrontation over economic growth and public welfare, despite widespread poverty at home. Ultimately, the Philippines will pay the price, Zheng said.

item.title: China-Europe freight train runs top 140,000 now, with total value of shipped goods exceeding $560 billion
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 13:26:00
A China-Europe freight train on the Yiwu-Xinjiang-Europe route leaves the East China International Intermodal Port in Jinhua, East China's Zhejiang Province on October 8, 2026. Photo: VCG As the X8059 China-Europe freight train bound for Moscow, Russia, departed from Shenyang, Northeast China's Liaoning Province, on Thursday, the cumulative number of China-Europe freight trains has surpassed 140,000 runs, with the total value of goods shipped exceeding $560 billion. The 140,000th freight train, X8059, carried household appliances, auto parts, and other goods. After departing from Shenyang Puhe Station, it is expected to arrive in Moscow in nine days. In recent years, the railway authorities did its best to expand the China-Europe freight train network to strengthen its radiating effect. Within China, they have fully utilized the western, central, and eastern corridors, with a total of 96 scheduled China-Europe freight train lines operating at 120 kilometer per hour within the country, connecting 132 Chinese cities. Abroad, the railway authorities have developed diversified overseas routes, with the service now reaching 237 cities in 26 European countries, and more than 100 cities in 12 Asian countries, covering the majority of Eurasia. According to data provided by China Railway Co, in May, the China-Europe freight trains topped 1,965 runs and transported 197,000 TEUs in that month, setting a new record high for monthly volume. Trains on the southern corridor have achieved regular operations, with 746 trains running from January to September, marking a year-on-year increase of 125 percent. A total of 22 full-timetable China-Europe freight trains now operate stably each week between nine Chinese cities and six European cities, precisely matching the cross-border transport needs of high-end manufacturing. As the service coverage and operational quality of the trains continue to improve, high-value-added goods such as automobiles and auto parts, machinery and equipment, and electronic and electrical products have become the main cargo sources for outbound trains. Meanwhile, European timber, pulp, specialty agricultural products, and daily consumer goods are rapidly entering the Chinese market via these trains, injecting new vitality into China-Europe trade. Currently, the railway authorities are advancing preparatory work for cross-border standard-gauge second-line projects at the Alashankou-Dostyk Port between China and Kazakhstan and the Manzhouli-Zabaykalsk port between China and Russia to further ramp up port throughput capacity. item.title: Von der Leyen's threat of tougher trade curbs on China is wrong prescription for Europe's industrial woes: experts
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 13:18:00
The European Union (EU) flags in front of EU headquarters in Brussels, Belgium. Photo: VCG European Commission (EC) President Ursula von der Leyen's renewed warnings of tougher trade measures against China, despite recent progress in bilateral negotiations, risk undermining hard-won agreements while doing little to address Europe's underlying industrial challenges, Chinese analysts said on Thursday, cautioning that trade pressure cannot substitute for industrial renewal. In a speech to the European Parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen said the bloc must be prepared to deploy “trade defense instruments” if dialogue [with China] fails to deliver results, even as she acknowledged progress in recent China-EU economic and trade consultations, according to a news released published on the EC’s website. She called for swift safeguard measures when import surges threaten European industries, citing growing concerns in the chemicals and machinery sectors. She also announced plans for a DiversifyEU package in December to reduce dependence on single suppliers, alongside a new instrument allowing the bloc to restrict access to its single market more quickly when its interests are threatened. EU's tougher posture reflects its struggle to adjust to a changing industrial landscape, particularly as Chinese manufacturers have gained ground in electric vehicles and other emerging industries, Wang Yiwei, director of Center for European Studies at Renmin University of China, told the Global Times on Thursday. Europe is seeking time to rebuild its industrial strength while facing pressure from member states and domestic industries, Wang said. “Trade restrictions may provide temporary relief, but cannot deliver the technological advances or industrial transformation needed for sustained growth.” The deeper challenge extends beyond individual products to the industrial systems and technologies shaping future manufacturing, which Europe needs to address by rebuilding its own capabilities rather than blaming China for its internal woes, according to Wang. Von der Leyen’s tougher rhetoric comes less than two weeks after Beijing and Brussels demonstrated that negotiations could deliver tangible results. During talks in Beijing on October 8-9, the two sides reached 16 points of consensus covering trade and investment, export controls, intellectual property and World Trade Organization reform. Von der Leyen credited EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic with progress, citing greater predictability in rare-earth export controls and an understanding on Chinese-made hybrid vehicle exports. She nevertheless claimed that progress in one sector could not resolve broader trade imbalances, according to the EC’s release. However, analysts warned that protectionism offers no lasting solution to Europe's industrial challenges, while continued trade pressure risks undermining the hard-won gains of China-EU negotiations. The EU's increasingly tough trade rhetoric also reflects its internal political dynamics. With 27 member states pursuing different industrial interests, Brussels faces considerable difficulties coordinating a common response, leaving it under pressure to demonstrate that it is standing up for European industries, Wang said. Even as the EU takes a harder line on trade, there is also recognition of the risks of escalating tensions with China. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday backed stronger EU trade defense tools to address so-called unfair competition from China. But he said the bloc did not want to make use of its trade defense toolbox, stressing that the goal was to achieve a new balance in trade rather than trigger a conflict, according to Bloomberg. The economic costs of greater trade restrictions were highlighted by Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Källenius, who warned on the same day that protectionist measures could raise production costs and distort global supply chains. While greater restrictions could improve resilience, they would also make production more expensive, he said, cautioning that Europe could not become "an island" cut off from major trading partners. Wang said Europe's heavy reliance on global markets and supply chains makes trade restrictions particularly costly. “European manufacturers depend on Chinese intermediate goods, while German automakers also produce vehicles in China for export,” he said, warning that such protectionist measures could end up working against Europe's own interests. Responding to reports that the EU was pursuing a "dual-track" approach of maintaining intensive consultations with China while stepping up restrictions, potentially including the use of its anti-coercion instrument, China's Ministry of Commerce said on October 16 that China-EU economic and trade consultations are intended to properly resolve differences through dialogue and accommodate each other's concerns. Both sides must demonstrate sincerity in resolving problems, the ministry said, stressing that the EU should not expect to gain benefits through pressure or underestimate China's determination and ability to safeguard its own interests. Meanwhile, channels for engagement remain open. According to a Euronews report on Wednesday, a delegation of 12 members of the European Parliament's Committee on International Trade will visit China from October 27 to 29 for talks with Chinese officials and lawmakers. Discussions are expected to cover market access, industrial subsidies, supply chains and critical raw materials. The EU should abandon geopolitical and confrontational thinking and make full use of the opportunities arising from China's innovation-driven development to expand cooperation in green development, new energy and digital industries for mutual benefit and win-win outcomes, Shi Xiaoli, director of the WTO Law Research Center at China University of Political Science and Law, told the Global Times.

item.title: China, Greece can draw on ancient civilizations to tackle modern challenges: Greek culture minister
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 11:17:00
Lina Mendoni, Minister of Culture of Greece at the press conference in Beijing on October 20, 2026 Photo: Dong Feng/Global Times China is home to the oldest civilization in the East, while Greece holds the oldest civilization in the West; both countries have made vital contributions to the development of civilization in their respective regions, a senior Greek official said at a recent press conference in Beijing. In today's turbulent world, marked by numerous challenges and upheavals, the wisdom embodied by these two great civilizations can offer essential and highly meaningful insights into addressing these issues, Lina Mendoni, Minister of Culture of Greece, who visited China for the 4th Liangzhu Forum, said at the press conference held by the Greek Embassy in China on Tuesday. Mendoni affirmed that China and Greece can promote mutual learning among civilizations and offer an exemplary model of peaceful coexistence and common development among different civilizations. China has the most ancient civilization in the East, while Greece has the most ancient civilization in the West, and both countries have made vital contributions to their respective regions, she said. "Today we're facing lots of challenges and upheavals. So our two classical civilizations can provide with their wisdom, very essential, very meaningful answers to today's problems. Even though our two civilizations did not come into great contact with each other, they do have lots of common elements, and thus our cooperation in the cultural field can produce even better results," said Mendoni. Ancient wisdom can offer answers to many contemporary problems, including climate change, or even the challenges we're facing due to new technologies. We can find answers in ancient wisdom, Mendoni said. The minister then highlighted key collaborative projects between Greece and China in cultural heritage and the digitalization of cultural relics. Mendoni told the Global Times that the cultural exchanges between the two countries have been ongoing for years. "I'd say that one of the main projects of cultural cooperation is organizing exhibitions in both countries, with Greek exhibitions in China and Chinese exhibitions in Greece." Greek people are familiar with and appreciate Chinese culture, and past Chinese exhibitions in Greece have been very successful, Mendoni said. She said the two countries are preparing for an exhibition of Chinese porcelain in Greece. "In the past, we had an exhibition at Acropolis Museum in Athens on Emperor Qianlong," Mendoni added. The exhibition From the Forbidden City: The Imperial Apartments of Qianlong was staged at Acropolis Museum in Athens, Greece, in mid-September 2018. It was a huge success, Mendoni stressed. "On the other side, we have had more than six exhibitions in China in the past few years that have attracted millions of visitors to date," Mendoni said. As for technological cooperation in digitalization of cultural relics, the minister expressed a positive view. "This cooperation extends also to our institutions, educational institutions and technical universities in Greece and China," said Mendoni, noting the interesting and important results of the scientific cooperation between the educational institutions and universities in the two countries.

item.title: Metamorphosis of a city that coal built, and nearly buried
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 09:28:00
People watch performances at a city park in Hegang City, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, June 20, 2026. (Xinhua) Li Jianguo, 72, remembers the mountain of coal waste that once loomed outside his front door. "Coal dust blew into the house with the wind all year round. You had to keep the windows shut even in summer," Li recalled. That was the nature of life in the city he knew for three decades as a coal miner. Today, the retiree strolls through a lakeside park every morning, thermos of tea in hand, watching children run across well-trimmed lawns while elderly neighbors practice Tai Chi under birch trees. The park is built on what was once a collapsed mining wasteland, a subsidence zone pockmarked with abandoned pits and shanties. In many ways, it tells the story of an entire city and its transformation. CITY BUILT ON "BLACK GOLD" The city of Hegang is located in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, near the Russian border, where forested hills give way to lowland plains. Though the city's name translates as crane ridge, it actually derives from an old word for the raccoon dogs that once roamed its wilderness. In 1914, a hunter accidentally found coal while clearing land along a river. A mining company was established four years later, drawing waves of mine workers. By 1929, a town had taken shape. Hegang got its present name when the People's Republic was founded in 1949, and went on to become one of new China's four major "coal capitals," an engine fueling the country's industrialization. But the "black gold" that gave birth to the city was finite. As reserves dried up and mines shut down one after another from the early 2000s onward, young people left, and Hegang became a city with far more homes than people. In 2019, the internet turned this surplus into a punchline. In one of the most extreme cases, an old walk-up apartment sold for just 15,000 yuan (2,246 U.S. dollars). Netizens joked that homes in Hegang were selling for "cabbage prices," meaning dirt cheap. "We were under huge pressure," said Xiao Yu, an official at the municipal bureau of housing and urban-rural development. Rather than doubling down on cheap housing to attract bargain hunters, the city chose to reverse course. Officials traveled across the country studying advanced building techniques, developed new construction standards tailored to extreme cold, and urged local developers to pursue quality over volume. Between 2019 and 2025, commercial housing sales grew nearly five-fold. Average prices at premium developments now exceed 4,800 yuan per square meter. "This is just the beginning," said Li Baiyang, chief of the municipal bureau of housing and urban-rural development. "We plan to upgrade all of Hegang's old housing into decent homes." This quiet, frigid city has its own appeal, especially for those fed up with the humid south or burned out by the whirlwind pace of life in megacities. Yan Bo and his wife, from the bustling city of Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, drove more than 2,000 kilometers to Hegang for a taste of its slower rhythm. They bought an apartment here and never left. Ivan, a Russian cross-border trader who asked that only his first name be used, settled here last year. He describes the city as "livable," and its people as "genuinely friendly." METAMORPHOSIS OF A CITY Hegang's transformation is even more dramatic than its housing market. A little over a decade ago, the city was still coated in soot. All its 16 waterways, including two rivers and 14 drainage channels, ran black with pollution. Years of systematic cleanup efforts have now turned them clear. The city demolished over 4,100 old buildings along riverbanks, planted 96 hectares of riverside greenery, and converted former mining subsidence zones into 32 parks and public squares. The deserted mine pit of Xinling has been renovated into a scenic area, and the Dulu River wetland has become an important stopover for migratory birds and home to some endangered species. A new economy is also taking shape underground. Hegang holds 2.3 billion tonnes of proven graphite ore, the raw material for lithium-ion battery anodes. More than 80 percent of China's natural graphite for battery production comes from here. The city has partnered with China Minmetals to apply modern technologies such as the Internet of Things and cloud computing across the whole graphite industrial chain, including mining and processing, and to overcome key technical hurdles in achieving high-purity graphite. The former coal capital is aiming to build a technological innovation highland for the graphite new materials industry. Chinese people have long held that food is the first pleasure of life. In Hegang, a traditional grain production base, that pleasure comes in the form of crayfish raised alongside rice paddies, and a signature street food: grilled meat skewers. This snack, popular since the 1950s when it provided quick calories for miners emerging from shifts, has grown into a 4.5-billion-yuan industry, with more than 1,200 franchise outlets across China. To foster further development, mayor Deng Weiyuan said the city will focus on upgrading traditional industries, cultivating emerging ones, and developing new quality productive forces tailored to local conditions. With a population of 935,000 and a modest GDP of 37.6 billion yuan in 2024, Hegang still faces many challenges. The shadow of the coal era lingers in old infrastructure and in the collective memory of its people. "Globally, resource-dependent cities face daunting transformation hurdles," said Sun Haojin, director of the Institute of Economics at the Heilongjiang Provincial Academy of Social Sciences. "Both economic restructuring and ecological improvement are difficult." He described Hegang's push for green development as exemplary. Like many rust-belt cities worldwide, Hegang is not so much reborn as it is being rebuilt. Its next chapter is being written by the people who stayed, and those who chose to arrive. Zheng Siduo, 32, graduated from a university in the provincial capital Harbin, and returned to his hometown to start a business. "Compared to the first-tier cities, Hegang's relaxed, livable and low-cost environment provides ideal soil for tech startups to grow," said Zheng, founder of Zhanhui Industrial Design, Hegang's first digital printing and creative design firm. The company, established in May this year, makes customized 3D-printed models and industrial components, exporting them globally via cross-border e-commerce platforms like Amazon. This photo taken on Sept. 2, 2026 shows the signature street food grilled meat skewers in Hegang City, northeast China's Heilongjiang Province. (Xinhua/Zhu Yue)

item.title: China-initiated Luban Workshops empower global youth with practical skills
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 08:09:00
Participants view exhibits at an exhibition during the World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference 2026 in Tianjin, north China, Oct. 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Ran) At an automotive industrial park in north China's Tianjin Municipality, Egyptian students Abdelrahman Ayman Zaky and Adham Ayman are gaining hands-on experience in new energy vehicle (NEV) chassis systems alongside their Chinese peers. Having acquired vocational skills at an Egyptian Luban Workshop, the two came to China to deepen their expertise. Adham, 20, hopes to improve his Chinese and vehicle maintenance skills before returning to Egypt to pursue a career as an automotive engineer. Their experience highlights the mission of the China-initiated Luban Workshops, which over the past decade have equipped young people worldwide with useful skills, fostered local talent, and supported industrial development. Named after Luban, an ancient Chinese craftsman and inventor who lived more than 2,500 years ago, the initiative draws on a longstanding Chinese tradition of craftsmanship and innovation. Jointly established by Chinese and foreign educational institutions, Luban Workshops now offer vocational education and skills-training programs in 32 countries. In Egypt, Luban Workshops are helping students like Adham translate classroom learning into engineering capabilities. Mohamed Mostafa, a student at an Egyptian Luban Workshop now studying at Tianjin Light Industry Vocational Technical College, said hands-on practice has strengthened his ability to tackle real-world engineering challenges. "In the EPIP (Engineering Practice and Innovation Project) classroom, we don't just work on simulated problems. We work on real-world engineering problems in teams, discussing solutions, refining our techniques and testing them again and again. We break down complex challenges to achieve the best results and meet engineering standards," Mostafa said. He added that he has shared the approach with students in Egypt, where they have applied the same methods to develop their own projects. The two Egyptian Luban Workshops have provided formal education to more than 3,100 people and skills training on over 4,000 occasions, creating new opportunities for industrial cooperation. Wang Baolong, dean of the School of Mechanical Engineering at Tianjin Light Industry Vocational Technical College, said graduates trained in advanced technologies can meet the needs of local businesses, strengthening Chinese companies' confidence in investing in and establishing factories in Egypt while supporting local economic development. An employment training base jointly established by the Egyptian Luban Workshops and the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone has provided young Egyptians with a direct pathway to employment. "After receiving professional technical training, these young people can operate production equipment proficiently. They are exactly the kind of skilled workers that companies need," Wang added. Beyond teaching technical skills, the workshops also help build local capacity for sustained vocational training. While setting up training centers and supplying advanced equipment, Chinese partners send teachers and technicians to train local instructors and arrange exchanges and learning opportunities in China. In 2016, the Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College and the Ayutthaya Technical College in Thailand jointly established the world's first Luban Workshop. Over the past decade, all six of the workshop's internationalized majors have been incorporated into Thailand's national education system. "We are not just cultivating talent for the local area, but leaving the whole system behind. Chinese standards and models are truly integrating into and promoting local development," said Mei Wentao, a staff member at the Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College. More than 100 Chinese companies in Thailand operate businesses ranging from NEV components to vehicle distribution. In August 2025, the China-Thailand automotive intelligent manufacturing industry-education integration community was established in Thailand. With a steady supply of skilled graduates, companies can recruit directly from schools, helping young Thai people find jobs more easily and quickly. In Central Asia, the Tajik Luban Workshop is helping local young people explore new career opportunities. In nearly four years of operation, it has provided learning and training opportunities to more than 3,600 undergraduate and postgraduate students. When Bakhtiyor Bozorzoda enrolled at the Tajik Technical University, he was uncertain about his chosen major in geodesy and cartography. Advanced surveying equipment, digital mapping technologies, and virtual simulation courses at the Tajik Luban Workshop helped him recognize the field's potential and develop a stronger interest in surveying. During his studies, Bozorzoda gained hands-on experience with high-precision instruments and digital mapping technologies. "I hope to continue my studies in China in the future, learn more advanced surveying technologies and contribute to infrastructure development in Tajikistan," he said. Today, Luban Workshops have become a hallmark of China's international vocational education cooperation. Data from China's Ministry of Education show that the country has established 38 Luban Workshops in 32 countries, providing formal education to more than 30,000 students and non-degree training to over 160,000 people. The Luban Workshops reflect a commitment to harmony, coexistence and the common good in Chinese cultural tradition. By responding to local needs, they help young people in different countries acquire skills that can benefit them throughout their careers, said Tian Xuejun, president of the China Education Association for International Exchange, at the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, held in Tianjin from Oct. 15 to 17. China has the world's largest vocational education system, with 9,151 secondary vocational schools, 1,554 higher vocational colleges and 124 vocational undergraduate institutions. As of the end of 2025, China's vocational education catalog covered 19 major categories, 97 subcategories and 1,491 majors, spanning virtually all sectors of the national economy and all 41 major industrial categories. China is continuing to strengthen its vocational education system to support the development of emerging industries and expand opportunities for people both at home and abroad. At the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, representatives from 45 countries jointly released the Framework of World Vocational and Technical Education Standards developed under China's leadership. The framework calls for improving vocational school systems, establishing lifelong education and training opportunities for all, developing teaching materials through industry-education collaboration, building teaching teams through school-enterprise partnerships, and using artificial intelligence to drive reform in education and teaching.

item.title: The Philippines should not misread the message of US warship's intrusion near Xianbin Jiao: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 22:59:00
The Philippines Illustration: Liu Rui/GT The US warship's early-morning "quick in, quick out" and the limited tonnage of a littoral combat ship themselves demonstrate that the priority of this performance was "risk control" rather than "deterrence effect." Any calculation that drawing in outside forces can help seize gains in the South China Sea is a serious misjudgment of the situation; any act that infringes on China's sovereignty and rights will be met with resolute countermeasures. In the early hours of Tuesday, the US littoral combat ship USS Charleston illegally intruded into the waters adjacent to Xianbin Jiao of China's Nansha Qundao without approval from the Chinese government. The People's Liberation Army (PLA) Southern Theater Command Navy dispatched forces to track and monitor the US vessel in accordance with laws and regulations. A spokesperson for the PLA Southern Theater Command Navy stated clearly that China holds indisputable sovereignty over Nansha Qundao and its adjacent waters. The US' action infringes upon China's sovereign rights and interests, jeopardizes maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability. The US side should immediately cease such activities. Xianbin Jiao lies to the east of Ren'ai Jiao. In recent years the Philippines has continuously taken infringement actions in the direction of Xianbin Jiao, hyped up the so-called "environmental issue" at Xianbin Jiao and dispatched coast guard vessels to illegally linger in its lagoon. These various moves have failed under China's countermeasures. At this moment, the US sent a littoral combat ship to intrude in the early morning. The action was carefully designed. The US warship's early-morning "quick in, quick out" and the limited tonnage of a littoral combat ship themselves demonstrate that the priority of this performance was "risk control" rather than "deterrence effect." So-called "freedom of navigation" is a false proposition in the South China Sea. The US' "freedom of navigation operations" are by no means intended to safeguard genuine freedom of navigation. Fifty percent of the world's merchant ships and one-third of maritime trade pass through the South China Sea. No matter how complex the disputes, normal international commercial navigation in the South China Sea has never been obstructed. What has truly turned "freedom of navigation" into an issue is not the passage needs of merchant ships, but the close-in disruptive actions of warships carrying specific political intentions. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) has still not clearly stipulated whether foreign warships enjoy the right of "innocent passage." Yet many countries require that foreign warships obtain approval or provide prior notification before entering their territorial seas. China also made relevant provisions in its 1992 Law on the Territorial Sea and the Contiguous Zone. Yet the US has not joined UNCLOS to this day, while believing that it has the "right to interpret" the Convention's concepts - this is itself a paradox. Observing the reactions of the US and the Philippines before and after the incident, one intruded and the other cheered. The US side trotted out its usual "freedom of navigation" rhetoric, while the Philippine side claimed that "the US warship did not intrude into Chinese territory." These "concerted performances" carried out in the name of fulfilling security commitments and upholding rules and order resemble a carefully choreographed parade, reflecting that the "display of allied strength" by the Philippines and the US in the South China Sea is nothing more than a publicity project staged around so-called "security issues." To some extent, such activities have become a "mobile billboard" for the US to showcase the credibility of its alliances. The audience this performance is aimed at may be other US allies and partners in the Asia-Pacific, proclaiming US military dominance in the region, but China remains an unavoidable "presence" in this performance. Anti-China forces within the Philippine military and police systems are now wantonly undermining China-Philippines relations. Behind this there is the backing and cheerleading of external forces, as well as the acquiescence and indulgence of the Philippine government. These people regard US "freedom of navigation" operations in the South China Sea as chips for gaming with China and for bargaining. But Manila needs to understand that external major powers will not bear the cost of direct conflict with China for the Philippines' adventurous actions, nor will they underwrite Manila when the situation gets out of control. They can withdraw at any time, and the Philippines will have to clean up the mess itself. Disputes in the South China Sea should be resolved through consultation among countries in the region; No external force has the right to intervene. This is a principle China has consistently upheld, and it is the only correct path for maintaining long-term peace and stability in the South China Sea. The Philippine side is advised not to misread the situation and mistake a performance for a "backer." The fact that this incident occurred in the early morning proves that any unauthorized infringement and intrusion is under China's monitoring and control. The Southern Theater Command Navy possesses all-weather situational awareness and rapid-response capabilities in the South China Sea, and is able to promptly detect, grasp, and handle relevant developments. China has indisputable sovereignty over the Nansha Qundao and their adjacent waters, and the Theater Command forces remain on high alert at all times. Manila needs to see clearly that the early-morning "quick in, quick out" performance by the US warship is not proof that "someone has its back," but rather a preview that "risks must be borne by oneself." Any calculation that drawing in outside forces can help seize gains in the South China Sea is a serious misjudgment of the situation; any act that infringes on China's sovereignty and rights will be met with resolute countermeasures.

item.title: Is Elon Musk building a 'flying car' because he has been 'pushed out' of traditional auto race by China?: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 21:47:00
Chinese NEVs Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT Editor's Note: Currently, China's economy is steadily advancing along the path of high-quality development, even as domestic and international circumstances become increasingly complex. Some Western media, due to misunderstanding or bias, have repeatedly questioned or even distorted China's economic development. Accordingly, the Global Times launches the "Q&A on China's Economy" column to publish opinion pieces to present facts and clarify perceptions. Tesla recently unveiled its next-generation Roadster, which can briefly take flight and perform an aerial flip, drawing global attention. The Wall Street Journal published an article arguing that "Elon Musk's latest vision for the company's sports car has more to do with China than cold-gas rocket thrusters." It suggested that Musk "is leaving the mainstream car market to the Chinese" because "many Western automakers are unable to compete without government intervention." The article also claimed that some Western automakers are feeling the same pressure as Musk to either "move up" or "be pushed out." But does the rise of China's auto industry really mean that automakers from other countries are being forced off the track? The competitive pressure generated by China's auto industry is indeed a reality that automakers around the world cannot ignore. Musk himself has publicly described Chinese automakers as the "most competitive in the world." According to the International Energy Agency, global electric vehicle sales exceeded 20 million in 2025, with Chinese automakers accounting for around 60 percent of sales and roughly three-quarters of global EV production. At this year's Paris Motor Show, the presence of more than 20 Chinese auto brands attracted considerable attention in Europe. Chinese companies have evolved from important participants in the global auto industry into formidable competitors in an expanding range of markets and technological fields. However, interpreting Tesla's Roadster unveiling as a simple retreat from the mainstream market is misleading. From the outset, the Roadster was designed for a niche market, serving as a showcase for Tesla's technological capabilities and brand image. It is not just Tesla. In recent years, nearly all leading global automakers have placed greater emphasis on autonomous driving, connected vehicles and AI applications, reflecting a broader industry consensus on the future of mobility and automotive technology. In fact, most established automakers have not abandoned the mass market. On the contrary, they are stepping up efforts to compete for this core segment of the automotive market. Volkswagen and Renault are still developing more affordable electric vehicles and Toyota and Honda are maintaining dual-track strategies involving both hybrids and pure electric vehicles. The transformation underway in the global auto industry is therefore far more complex than a scenario in which Chinese companies take over the mass market while Western automakers retreat to the premium segment. To understand this transformation, it is essential to examine the sources of China's automotive competitiveness. Technological innovation in the auto industry has often followed a pattern in which new technologies are introduced in premium models before gradually spreading to ordinary vehicles. The more advanced the technology, the higher the price tends to be. As the technology matures and becomes more widely available, features once reserved for high-end cars eventually find their way into more affordable models. The intense competition in China's auto market is accelerating this process. In 2025, around 70 percent of the battery electric vehicles sold in China were priced below the average price of conventional gasoline cars. Smart cockpits, advanced driver-assistance systems, efficient electric drivetrains and ultra-fast charging are increasingly available in vehicles that ordinary consumers can afford. Whether Musk's "flying sports car" will ever prove practical remains to be seen. China's auto industry, however, has already demonstrated that new technologies need not be reserved for a privileged few; they can also benefit the wider public. The fundamental strength of China's auto industry lies in its ability to closely integrate technological innovation, large-scale manufacturing and market demand, enabling advanced technologies to be translated into products more quickly and made accessible to more consumers. This is underpinned by the country's long-developed industrial ecosystem. Close coordination across the power battery, electric motor, electronic controls and intelligent manufacturing sectors allows automakers to iterate technologies and develop new products more rapidly. China's vast domestic market provides a wealth of real-world application scenarios, while consumers' growing demand for intelligent and electrified vehicles continues to push companies to improve their products. Chinese automakers also face intense competition, and a number of new-energy vehicle companies have already been eliminated in recent years. Yet it is this competitive environment that has helped drive greater industrial efficiency and innovation, propelling the sector to the forefront of the global industry. Seen in this light, portraying the growth of China's auto industry as "swallowing up markets" deliberately amplifies the perceived threat of competition while overlooking the new opportunities and changes that healthy competition can create. Tesla's entry into China injected fresh competition into the domestic market, producing a "catfish effect" that spurred local manufacturers to improve. The establishment of Tesla's Shanghai Gigafactory also put pressure on Chinese automakers, but Chinese suppliers gained technical expertise and experience through production partnerships, improving both efficiency and quality. This has been a process of mutual development. Today, cooperation between Chinese and international automakers, such as Xpeng and Volkswagen, as well as Geely and Ford, further demonstrates how the global auto industry is building new networks of innovation. More than a century of automotive history has been a story of competition driving innovation and technology becoming increasingly accessible. The US once revolutionized the industry through mass production; Japanese automakers raised efficiency through lean manufacturing; and European carmakers built deep strengths in technology and branding. Today, the rise of China's auto industry is adding a new chapter to that history. Rather than treating market competition as a zero-sum game in which one side's gains must come at the other's expense, automakers should focus on strengthening their competitiveness through innovation and cooperation. China's automotive rise has not deprived the global auto industry of a future. On the contrary, it has opened up more possibilities for the industry's future.

item.title: GT Voice: Chip export boom reveals deepening China-South Korea complementarity
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 20:47:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT South Korea's exports are becoming a showcase of the global technology industry. During the first 20 days of October, South Korea's semiconductor exports surged 222.5 percent year-on-year to reach $27.5 billion, setting a new record. The chip exports accounted for 44.7 percent of the country's total, up 16.2 percentage points from a year earlier, the Yonhap News Agency reported on Wednesday. By destination, chip exports to China soared 154.4 percent to $16.6 billion, and exports to the US stood at $10.7 billion. Viewed over the longer term, this round of South Korea's export growth extends an AI-driven expansion of global computing demand that has been building for years. In 2024, South Korean chip exports rose to $141.9 billion, up 43.9 percent year-on-year. In 2025, the figure climbed to $173.4 billion, up 22.2 percent. South Korea's semiconductor exports have kept surging this year. In the first quarter, they reached $78.5 billion, up 139 percent year-on-year, and in the first half year, they hit $192.4 billion, exceeding the whole of 2025. The Bank of Korea in August raised the country's economic growth forecast this year to 3.3 percent - an increase of 0.7 percentage points and the highest level since 2021. The rationale behind this upward revision was that the extraordinary prosperity of South Korea's semiconductor sector was spreading from exports into domestic consumption, investment and other areas of local demand, steering the country's economy onto a more solid trajectory of growth. The massive jump in South Korea's exports to China stands out. At $16.6 billion, the figure far outpaces the value of shipments to the US. This export pattern reflects two things. On one hand, China's ongoing investment in AI large-language model training, data center construction and digital infrastructure is unleashing enormous demand for memory chips. On the other, Asia's regional semiconductor supply chain retains remarkable resilience despite geopolitical disturbances outside the region. The deep complementarity between the Chinese and South Korean technology industries rests on solid structural foundations. China is one of the world's largest semiconductor markets, with integrated circuit imports rising 63.5 percent year-on-year to $499 billion in the first nine months of this year. Samsung and SK Hynix together hold roughly 70 percent of the global memory chip supplies, and both companies' Chinese plants are deeply embedded in local supply chains. With the world's largest demand market on one side and irreplaceable high-end supply on the other, this deeply intertwined pattern, where each side is present in the other's industrial landscape, is not something that external factors can easily change. But challenges remain behind the eye-catching data. South Korea's chip exports are mostly concentrated in the memory sector. At the same time, the technology export controls implemented by certain countries pose potential risks too. This is precisely why both the space and necessity for deeper China-South Korea industrial chain cooperation are on the rise. If South Korea hopes to translate its current export momentum into sustainable long-term growth, relying solely on technological upgrades and product iteration will not be enough. The more important step lies in proactive industrial chain-level planning, deepening coordination with the broader Asian semiconductor ecosystem, and above all, preserving and expanding the depth of cooperation with China. This is a strategic issue that will determine whether South Korea can retain sufficient room for maneuver in an increasingly fragmented global trade environment. The 17th round of negotiations on Phase II of the China-South Korea Free Trade Agreement, held in Seoul last week, placed services and investment at the core of discussions. This suggests that the two sides may open greater room for institutional opening-up in information technology, high-end manufacturing and the digital economy, extending semiconductor complementarity currently concentrated in goods trade into other fields. Over the medium and long term, complementarity between the Chinese and South Korean industrial chains is far from reaching its ceiling. As global technology supply chains continue to face considerable uncertainty, deeper cooperation grounded in market logic and industrial reality will not only sustain South Korea's export curve, but also inject greater stability into the regional economy.
